title: M/S Bhartiya Hindu Shudhi vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka on 16 February, 2022
full_text: M/S Bhartiya Hindu Shudhi vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka on 16 February, 2022 IN THE COURT OF SH. AJAY NAGAR, ADDITIONAL RENT CONTROLLER-02 (CENTRAL), TIS HAZARI COURTS, DELHI. CNR No.DLCT03-003145/2015 ARC No: 80184/16 E.No-80/17/15 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Shudhi Sabha Trust (Regd.), Through its Honorary Secretary/ President/Manager, Shudhi Sabha Bhawan, 6949, Birla Lines, Subzi Mandi Delhi-110007. ......Petitioner VERSUS Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka S/o Sh. H.R Loyalka C/o 2/1, First Floor, Singh Sabha Road, Ghanta Ghar, Delhi-110006. ......Respondent Date of filing : 16.09.2015 Date of Judgment : 16.02.2022 JUDGMENT Digitally signed by AJAY AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:24:23 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 1 1. Brief facts of the present case is that on 16.09.2015, petitioner filed present petition Under Section 14 (1) (a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (hereinafter referred to as " DRC Act ") praying to this court to pass an order of eviction in favour of the petitioner and against the respondent in respect of half portion of the ground floor measuring 57.26 square meters and open covered area (shed type) measuring 42.75 square meters situated on the ground floor of the property bearing No.6949, Birla Lines, Delhi- 110007 more specifically shown in Red colour in the attached site plan. (hereinafter referred to as "tenanted premises"). 2. It is inter-alia averred by the petitioner that respondent lastly paid the rent till 31.08.2012 @ Rs.1111/- p.m.; by virtue of notice dated 22.04.2015 rent was increased by 10% and at present rate of rent is Rs.1222/- p.m. w.e.f. 01.06.2015 onwards; tenanted premises was let out to respondent by two lease deeds dated 12.01.1972 and 01.01.1974; respondent is liable to pay rent w.e.f. 01.09.2012 @ Rs.1111/- p.m. and w.e.f. 01.06.2015 onwards @ Rs.1222/- p.m.; legal demand notice dated 22.04.2015 has not been complied with by the respondent; legal demand notice sent but received back with the report of undelivered. Lastly, it is prayed by the petitioner that present petition may be allowed. 3. Written statement was filed by the respondent inter-alia Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:24:48 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 2 stating that legal demand notice dated 22.04.2015 has never been served upon the respondent; the same is not correctly addressed; respondent is residing at 2/1, First Floor, Singh Sabha Road, Ghanta Ghar, Delhi which is correctly mentioned in the title of present petition; the contents of paragraph no.1 to 4 are not disputed; the petitioner has fabricated the legal demand notice as the same was never dispatched and served upon the respondent; petitioner chose to manufacture this address knowingly that respondent is not available there to receive this notice; it is wrong and denied that respondent has not paid or tendered the rent qua tenanted premises w.e.f. 01.09.2012 @ Rs. 1111/- p.m. and w.e.f. 01.06.2015 at Rs.1222/- p.m.; present petition is not maintainable in the absence of service of legal demand notice. Lastly, it is prayed by the respondent that the present petition may be dismissed with cost. 4. In the replication, the petitioner has denied the averments in the written statement and has reiterated his stand as taken in the petition. it is inter-alia averred in the replication that proper address of the tenanted premises is mentioned on the legal demand notice; notice was posted on the tenanted premises in occupation of the tenant/respondent; it is no where mentioned in any of the documents that for the purposes of service of the notice or summons, respondent is living at 2/1, First Floor, Singh Sabha Road, Ghanta Ghar, Delhi; tenanted premises have been correctly shown in the notice. Lastly, it Digitally signed by AJAY AJAY NAGAR NAGAR Date: 2022.02.16 12:25:00 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 3 is prayed by the petitioner that eviction petition may be allowed. 5. The petitioner has examined PW1 Sh. Surinder Kumar and relied upon several documents and he was cross examined at length and thereafter P.E was closed. 6. It is pertinent to mention that an order U/S 15(1) of DRC Act was passed by Ld. Predecessor of this court on 03.10.2016 directing the respondent to deposit the rent w.e.f. 01.09.2012 till 31.05.2015 @ Rs.1111/- p.m. and thereafter from 01.06.2015 till the date of order @ Rs.1222/- p.m. along with interest at 15% p.a. within a month from the date of order in the bank account of the petitioner. The respondent was further directed to deposit future rent month by month by the 15th day of each month in the bank account of the petitioner. It is also pertinent to mention that on 10.10.2019, one application U/S 15(7) DRC Act was allowed by the Ld. Predecessor of this court and thereby struck out the defence of the respondent. In consequence thereof, no evidence has been allowed to be led by the respondent. 7. I have heard the argument advanced. I have carefully gone through the pleadings, documents, testimonies, written Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:25:14 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 4 arguments, case law relied upon and the material on record. (i) Landlordship:- 8. Perusal of petition shows that the petitioner has claimed to be landlord and owner of the tenanted premises on the basis of documents Ex. PW1/2. On the other hand, the respondent has not specifically disputed the landlordship of the petitioner as he has stated that the contents of paragraph No. 1 to 4 are not disputed. As such, the respondent has admitted to be tenant in the tenanted premises and he has also admitted the petitioner as his landlord. As such, there exist the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. (ii) Legal demand notice:- 9. Perusal of petition shows that the petitioner has claimed to have sent legal demand notice dated 22.04.2015 Ex PW1/6 upon respondent prior to filing of present petition. On the other hand, respondent has vehemently disputed the service of such legal demand notice upon him. The plea of the respondent is that such legal demand notice was deliberately not addressed properly and it was not sent on his residential address i.e. 2/1 first floor Singh sabha road, Ghanta Ghar Delhi which is correctly mentioned in the title of the present petition. On the other hand, in the replication, the petitioner has claimed that it was sent on the correct address. AJAY Digitally signed by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:25:25 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 5 10. I have carefully gone through the pleadings, documents and material on record. 11. Perusal of record shows that the address of tenanted premises as mentioned in paragraph No. 8 of the petition is ground floor of the property No. 6949, Birla lines Delhi- 110007 and even in the prayer of the petition, the same address has been mentioned. 12. I have gone through the legal demand notice as well as post receipt Ex. PW1/7. Perusal of these documents shows that the address of tenanted premises has been mentioned in these documents. As such, it is clear from the record that the legal demand notice was directed to the tenanted premises. Now the plea of the respondent is that such legal notice should have been sent on this residential address and not on the tenanted premises. 13. In the case titled as Ajay Ahuja & Anr. vs M/S Subhiksha Trading Services in CS(OS) No. 241/2010 decided on 3 December, 2010, the hon'ble High Court Of Delhi observed as under:- "14. The next question which comes up for consideration in this case is as to whether the notice, whereby the tenancy of the defendant was sought to be terminated by the plaintiffs, can be said to have been duly issued to/served on them. Admittedly, the notice was not actually received by the defendant-company either at its corporate office or at the suit premises. The notice sent by courier was received back with the remarks "shifted", whereas the Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka NAGAR 62022.02.16 12:25:39 +0530 notice sent by registered post at the suit premises was received back with the remarks "on repeated visits premises found locked". As noted earlier, the notice sent at the registered office of defendant-company was also sent with the remarks "left without instructions". 15. The contention of the learned counsel for the plaintiff is that the plaintiffs did whatever they could possibly have done to serve the notice upon the defendants and if the defendants chose to lock the suit premises and either shift its registered office or altogether stop its functioning and close down its operations and its registered office, without any intimation to the plaintiffs, that would amount to deliberate avoidance to receive the notice and consequently constitute a valid service. 16. In M/s. Madan and Co. Vs. Wazir Jaivir Chand AIR 1989, SC 630, the notice sent by the landlord to the tenant by registered post was received back with the endorsement "left without address returned to sender". The relevant statutory provision which in the case before Supreme Court was Section 12 of J&K Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 provided for receipt of a notice of demand of rent by the tenant. The question which came up for consideration before the Court was as to whether the notice sent by registered post could be said to have been served and the tenant could be said to have received it. It was observed by the Court all that a landlord can do to comply with the requirement of sending notice is to post a pre-paid registered letter, containing the tenants correct address, and once he does this and the letter is delivered to the post office, he has no control over it. It is then presumed to have been delivered to the addressee under Section 27 of General Clauses Act. It was further observed that a tenant can so many manipulate the matters that the notice gets returned to the sender with vague endorsement such as "not found" "not in station", "addressee has left" and so on. It was contended before the Court that a landlord knowing that the tenant is away from the station for some reasons, could go through the motions of posting a letter to him which he knows will be served. Recognizing such a possibility, the Court was of the view that if a registered letter, addressed to a person at his Digitally signed by AJAY AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 7 12:25:57 +0530 residential address does not get served in the normal course and is returned, it can only be attributed to the addressees own conduct and that if he is compelled to be away for some time, all that he has to do is leave necessary instructions with the postal authorities either to detain the letters addressed to him for some times until he returns or to forward them to the address where has gone or to deliver them to some other person authorized by him. 17. In K. Bhaskaran Vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan and Another , (1999) 7 SCC 510, the notice sent under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, was returned with the endorsement "addressee absent" and "intimation served on addressees house". Observing that giving of notice is distinguished from receiving of notice, it was observed by Supreme Court that a person gives notice to another by taking such steps as may be reasonably required to inform the other in the ordinary course, whether or not such other actually comes to know of it. It was further observed that if a strict interpretation is given that the drawer should have actually received the notice, for the period of 15 days to start running, no matter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by different strategies and he could escape from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act. It was held that when a notice is returned by the sender as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date for reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in Clause (c) to the proviso of Section 138 of the Act. Of course such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. In the case before this Court the defendant has not come forward to contest the suit and to claim that it had no knowledge of the notice sent by the plaintiffs and was not in any manner responsible for its non-service. 18. In D. Vinod Shivappa Vs. Nanda Belliappa (2006) 6 SCC 456, Supreme Court while dealing with a notice issued under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act and sent by registered post inter alia observed as under: "This leaves us with the third situation where the notice Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka NAGAR 8 2022.02.16 12:26:10 +0530 could not be served on the addressee for one or the other reason, such as his non availability at the time of delivery, or premises remaining locked on account of his having gone elsewhere etc. etc. If in each such case the law is understood to mean that there has been no service of notice, it would completely defeat the very purpose of the Act. It would then be very easy for an unscrupulous and dishonest drawer of a cheque to make himself scarce for sometime after issuing the cheque so that the requisite statutory notice can never be served upon him and consequently he can never be prosecuted." In V. Raja Kumari Vs. P. Subbarama Naidu and Anr 2004 8 SCC 774, dealing with a case where the notice could not b served on account of the fact that the door of the house of the drawer was found locked, Supreme Court held that the principle incorporated in Section 27 of General Clauses Act will apply to a notice sent by post and it would be for the drawer to prove that it was not really served and he was not responsible for such non-service. In State of M.P. Vs. Hiralal and Ors 1996 (7) SCC 523, the respondent managed to have the notice returned with postal remarks "not available in the house", "house locked" and " shot closed". It was held that the notices had been served on the respondents. In C.C. Alavi Haji Vs. Palapetty Muhammed and Anr. 2007 6 SCC 555, a Three-Judges Bench of Supreme Court was called upon to re-consider an earlier decision of Two- Judges Bench in the case of D. Vinod (supra), Supreme Court reiterated that where the payee despatches the notice by registered post with correct address of the drawer of cheque, the principle incorporated in Section 27 of General Clauses Act would be attracted. During the course of the judgment, the Court, inter alia, observed as under: " Section 27 gives rise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post. In view of the said presumption, when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that in spite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice. Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 9 12:26:20 +0530 effected at the time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business." 19. In the case before this Court also, it was for the defendant-company, if it decided to lock the suit premises which it had been taken on rent from the plaintiffs, to make necessary arrangements for service of the letters, etc that could be sent to it, either by instructing the postal authorities to re-direct those letters to another address or to make some other arrangement for receipt of letters, etc. on its behalf. Same would be the position with respect to the registered office of the defendant-company, if it had decided to change its registered office or to altogether close down its operations as well as its registered office, without shifting the same to another place, (though as long as a company exists, it must have a registered office), it ought to have either provided an alternative address to the postal authorities for re-directing its letter to that address or should have made some alternative arrangement for receipt of letters, etc. sent to its registered office. Another option available to the defendant-company was to give public notice communicating its new address to the public at large and/or to all those with whom it had transected any business, including its debtors and creditors as well as the landlords of the premises which it had taken on rent. If the defendant-company decided not to adopt any of these courses available to it, the plaintiffs cannot be blamed for non-receipt of the notice by the defendant-company. The plaintiffs did the best they could have done by sending notice by registered post not only at the suit premises, but also at the registered office of the defendant-company and in these circumstances, the statutory presumption under Section 27 of General Clauses Act with respect to service of notice sent by registered post cannot be denied to the plaintiffs. 20. I, therefore, have no hesitation in holding that by sending the notice dated 11 th November, 2009 which was returned back with the remarks "shirted" "on repeated visits premises found locked" and "left without instructions" the plaintiffs have duly complied with the requirement of Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act." Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:26:31 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 10 14. In the considered view of this court, the tenanted premises was appropriate address for the purpose of the service of legal demand notice, particularly when, no notice in writing was given by the respondent to the petitioner in respect of his new address for the purposes of notice and summons. The petitioner is not supposed to send the notice of demand on the every address of the respondent. Moreover, nothing has been proved by the respondent that the petitioner was given notice in writing about the new address on which he was to receive the legal demand notice. Moreover, it was the duty of the respondent to inform the Indian post department about his availability on the other address but nothing has been done by the respondent. In the considered view of this court, respondent cannot take advantage of his own default or negligence. Moreover, as discussed earlier, no evidence at all has been led by the respondent in the present case as the defence of the respondent was already struck out under section 15(7) of DRC Act. 15. Record shows that the respondent has relied upon certain case law. But the same does not assist the respondent in view of peculiar facts of the present case, well settled proposition of law and also the exhaustive reasons as given earlier. As such, there is deemed service of the legal demand notice upon the respondent. Digitally signed by AJAY AJAY NAGAR NAGAR Date: 2022.02.16 12:26:42 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 11 (iii) Non-payment of rent:- 16. Petition shows that the petitioner has claimed that the respondent is in arrears of rent w.e.f. 01.09.2012 to 31.05.2015 at Rs 1111/- per month and w.e.f. 01.06.2015 at the rate of Rs. 1222/ per month. On the other hand, respondent has denied such averments in para No. 18 (a) of the written statement. The Written statement shows that the respondent has merely denied such averments of petition and has not given the details about payment of such rent to the petitioner. It is well settled that it is the duty of the respondent/ tenant to prove that he or she has already paid the entire rent and noting is outstanding against him. But in the present petition, respondent has failed to prove even prime facie that he paid the entire rent to the petitioner as nothing at all has been disclosed even in the written statement about such payment of rent. The entire defence of respondent is that service of legal demand notice has not been effected upon him. Record shows that no evidence has been led by the respondent to prove the payment of rent to the petitioner. Moreover, it is also not of the case of the respondent that the legal demand notice was duly complied with by him within two months. As such this ingredient is also satisfied. Conclusion:- 17. In view of exhaustive reasons and material on record, the Petitioner has been able to satisfy all the ingredients of section 14(1) Digitally signed by AJAY AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:26:55 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 12 (a) of DRC Act . Accordingly, the petition under section 14 (1)(a) of DRC Act is allowed. 18. It is pertinent to mention that an order U/S 15(1) of DRC Act was passed by Ld. Predecessor of this court on 03.10.2016 directing the respondent to deposit the rent w.e.f. 01.09.2012 till 31.05.2015 @ Rs.1111/- p.m. and thereafter from 01.06.2015 till the date of order @ Rs.1222/- p.m. along with interest at 15% p.a. within a month from the date of order in the bank account of the petitioner. The respondent was further directed to deposit future rent month by month by the 15th day of each month in the bank account of the petitioner. 19. In view of the material on record and discussion as earlier, there is no need to pass the modified order U/Sec. 15(1) D.R.C. Act. 20. Nazir is directed to file his report on the date as mentioned in separate order sheet regarding compliance of the order passed under section 15(1) of DRC Act. 21. Perusal of record shows that the defence of the respondent was struck off u/s 15 (7) of DRC Act by Ld. Predecessor of this court as respondent failed to make payment in compliance with Digitally signed AJAY by AJAY NAGAR Date: NAGAR 2022.02.16 12:27:05 +0530 ARC No. 80184/16 M/s Bhartiya Hindu Vs Sh. Shashi Kant Loyalka 13 the order u/s 15 (1) of DRC Act. However, this aspect shall be dealt with separately by this court while ascertaining whether the respondent is entitled to the benefit u/s 14 (2) of DRC Act or not. 22. Miscellaneous file be prepared for ascertaining the benefits U/Sec. 14(2) of the D.R.C. Act. 23. This file be consigned to Record Room after due compliance.
